digest.top_line: Brain SRS MRI review: imaging-to-treatment interval ≥14 days tied to 6-mo LC 56% vs 95% (Seymour); <1 mm total distortion and vendor 3D correction set as minimums.
digest.tldr: No new trial readouts today; this is a day of practice references. CNS carried most of it: an SRS MRI review ties a ≥14-day imaging-to-treatment interval to 6-mo LC 56% vs 95%, and a three-center single-isocenter multimet reference says fractionate if a lesion is >2-3 cm or V12 >10 cm3. Skin covers hypofractionated NMSC (LC 90-100%). Breast slides recap Z11 10-yr de-escalation.

sites.intro: Low-evidence pieces: a hypofractionation position paper built on observational cohorts and a single-pt HDR mould case report.

studies.name: HDR Surface Mould Brachytherapy for Eyelid Carcinoma
studies.tldr: 52 Gy/13 fx HDR surface mould (4 Gy BID) after excision of eyelid sebaceous carcinoma: disease-free at 6 mo, mild dry eye only.

🔍 MRI face/neck: no residual disease, no significant lymphadenopathy

📊 No acute side effects across weekly review for 9 consecutive weeks
⚠️ OAR doses stated only as 'within tolerable limits' (Fig 3D); no lens or lacrimal numbers in text
⚠️ Adjuvant scar target with no gross disease: 6-mo disease-free status does not test tumor control
⚠️ α/β behind the EQD2 conversion not stated in source
🔗 Authors cite GEC-ESTRO preference for brachy over EBRT for small-volume skin targets

verdict.rationale: Single-pt case report with 6-mo follow-up, adjuvant scar target without gross disease. Feasibility only; authors note no cohort or randomized data exist.
verdict.audience: Post-excision eyelid sebaceous carcinoma, margin status unknown, no residual

studies.significance: The transferable content is the build: a wax-wrapped 5-mm lead shield under the lid, a wax dummy for CT, CTV = scar + 1 cm with no PTV, and 4 Gy BID 6 hours apart to 52 Gy. OAR doses appear only as 'within tolerable limits' (Fig 3D), so lens and lacrimal dose cannot be benchmarked from the source text.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with a small eyelid sebaceous carcinoma after excision with unknown margins and no residual disease on MRI who declines re-excision or an interstitial implant, this supports surface mould HDR as a feasible adjuvant option; it does not extend to gross or node-positive disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Single-patient case report** with a step-by-step technical description and **weekly review for 9 consecutive weeks**. Follow-up **6 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: 54-yo woman, **0.8 cm × 0.5 cm** lesion of the R upper eyelid near the lateral canthus, IHC consistent with **localized sebaceous carcinoma** (Ki-67 30%-40%). Excisional biopsy with **margin status not reported**; MRI showed no residual disease and no significant lymphadenopathy.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: HDR surface mould, **52 Gy/13 fx at 4 Gy BID**, 6 hours apart, Ir-192; EQD2 **60.67 Gy**, equated by the authors to 60 Gy LDR. **CTV = scar + 1 cm**, no PTV margin, with a 5-mm wax-wrapped lead shield under the lid at each fraction. Chosen over electrons for sharper dose fall-off and lower penetration, and over interstitial brachy as non-invasive.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: CTV 0.71 mL, D90 4 Gy, DNR **0.26** (limit < 0.36). **Disease-free at 6 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No acute side effects**; **mild dry eye** the only effect reported at last review. OAR doses described only as within tolerable limits, with numbers confined to Fig 3D.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Authors tabulate prior surface-mould eyelid series (Guix, Montero, Vavassori, Jain) and cite one systematic review that found no randomized or cohort data. The extracted comparison table does not reliably pair values to series, so per-series outcomes cannot be cited here.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-excision localized eyelid sebaceous carcinoma with unknown margins and no residual disease on MRI. Does not represent gross, thick, or node-positive eyelid tumors.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: OAR doses not reported numerically in text; α/β for the LDR-equivalence calculation not stated. Follow-up too short for late lens, lacrimal or lid toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Value is the reproducible procedure, not the outcome: one adjuvant pt cannot speak to control of macroscopic disease. **Late ocular effects** of a 4 Gy BID schedule remain the open cost.

studies.interpretation:
This is a single-patient technical report, and its value lies in the procedure rather than the outcome. The case is also not quite the one the title implies: the lesion had already been excised, MRI showed no residual disease, and the indication for RT was a margin status nobody reported. Treating a scar plus 1 cm in a pt without gross disease is adjuvant therapy, so the 6-month disease-free status says little about whether surface mould HDR controls a visible eyelid tumor. A reader weighing mould brachytherapy for macroscopic disease should look to the prior series the authors tabulate, not to this case.

Against prior data, the authors name the surface-mould eyelid series of Guix, Montero, Vavassori and Jain, plus a single systematic review that itself found no randomized or cohort studies. The GEC-ESTRO working group position favouring brachytherapy over external beam for small skin targets is the strongest support cited, and it is a recommendation, not a comparative outcome. The comparison table in the source does not reliably tie values to individual series, so per-series control or dose figures cannot be drawn from it here. The evidence base therefore remains small retrospective series and expert opinion. This case adds one pt with sebaceous carcinoma, a histology the authors rank behind BCC and SCC in frequency.

The dose rationale rests on matching 52 Gy in 13 fractions to 60 Gy LDR, with an EQD2 of 60.67 Gy. The α/β behind that conversion is not stated, and an equivalence built around tumor response says little about late effects in the lens, lacrimal gland and cornea. For those tissues, 4 Gy per fraction delivered twice daily 6 hours apart is the parameter a skeptic would question first, since late-responding normal tissue may not fully repair within that interval. OAR doses are described only as within tolerable limits, with the numbers in a figure, so a reader cannot check lens or lacrimal dose against their own constraints. Plan-quality metrics are given (CTV 0.71 mL, D90 at the 4 Gy per-fraction prescription, DNR 0.26 against a limit of 0.36), and the internal lead shield wrapped in wax to reduce backscatter is the practical detail most departments would want to copy.

What it does not settle: 6 months is too short for the late ocular effects that define the cost of eyelid RT, and mild dry eye at that point may not be the final toxicity picture. Whether surface mould spares the eye better than electrons in practice, or matches interstitial control for thicker lesions, cannot be judged from one superficial post-excision target. The decision it informs is narrow. For a pt who declines re-excision or an implant after an excision with uncertain margins, a non-invasive mould with an internal lead shield is a workable adjuvant option, and the step list is a usable template for a department setting one up.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The transferable content is the build: wax-wrapped 5-mm lead shield under the lid, wax dummy for CT, CTV = scar + 1 cm with no PTV, 4 Gy BID 6 hours apart to 52 Gy. OAR doses appear only as 'within tolerable limits' (Fig 3D), so lens and lacrimal dose cannot be benchmarked from source text.

open_questions: Late lens, lacrimal and lid toxicity of 4 Gy BID beyond 6 mo
Surface mould control for gross eyelid tumors vs adjuvant scar targets
Surface mould vs electrons or interstitial brachy for eyelid carcinoma

studies.significance: The bigger de-escalation is in the Table 1 footnote: observation rather than adjuvant RT for most BCCs and low-risk SCCs, framed as an omission question, not a fractionation one. The schedule menu goes beyond RCR's modest trim (50 Gy in 15 fx instead of 55 Gy in 20 fx), and the author keeps PNI fields and high-risk lower lip SCC as exceptions at 20 or 25 fractions.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt over 80 or ECOG 2/3 with localised BCC or SCC, this expert opinion supports a 1–4 fraction course (e.g. 28 Gy in 4 fx twice weekly) over protracted schedules; it does not extend to PNI fields or high-risk lower lip SCC.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Single-author point-of-view** (JMIRO 2020), no new pt data. Cites a systematic review of **40 publications, over 12 000 NMSC**, plus RCR COVID-19 guidance.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Proposes **≤15 fractions** (definitive or adjuvant) for most pts and **1–4 fractions** as the default over 80 or ECOG 2/3. Cited review: mean **38 Gy, 8 Gy per fraction, 3 times per week**; similar BED assumed at α/β = 10 across schedules.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RCR (UK) trimmed fractions modestly: **40 Gy in 8 fx instead of 10**, **50 Gy in 15 fx instead of 55 Gy in 20 fx**. This piece pushes further, especially for pts over 80 and the adjuvant setting.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents localised BCC and SCC treated definitively or adjuvantly, especially elderly or ECOG 2/3 pts. Does not represent PNI fields encompassing neural structures or high-risk lower lip SCC, where 20 or 25 fractions may be justified.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The evidence base is **predominantly observational with very few RCTs**, and the cited review pooled heterogeneous pts and techniques. No late cosmesis data is offered for pts under 70, the group whose fractionation the argument would also shorten.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The argument holds that because LC is **>90–95%** with any technique, fraction number becomes a burden and resource question. It leaves open whether **omitting adjuvant RT** is safe beyond low-risk SCC.

studies.interpretation:
The argument rests on an asymmetry the author states directly. NMSC is radioresponsive enough that definitive RT by almost any technique gives LC above 90–95%, while the late cutaneous effects that justify protracted 2–2.5 Gy courses matter less as age rises and performance status falls. If control is largely insensitive to schedule within the ranges used, then fraction number becomes a question of resources and pt burden, not efficacy. On that reading the pandemic did not create the case for hypofractionation. It exposed a case the elderly, comorbid referral population already made.

The evidence offered rests on two supports. The cited systematic review of 40 publications and over 12 000 lesions reports a mean of 38 Gy in 8 Gy fractions three times weekly, with LC of 90-100% for hypofractionated RT. RCR COVID-19 guidance trimmed fractions only modestly, with 40 Gy in 8 fractions rather than 10 and 50 Gy in 15 rather than 55 Gy in 20. This piece goes further than RCR, proposing ≤15 fractions for most pts and 1–4 fractions as the default over 80 or ECOG 2/3. That gap is the thing to weigh. RCR adjusted at the margin, and this piece argues the margin itself is set wrong for much of the caseload.

Confidence should be tempered by what the author concedes: the base is predominantly observational cohorts with very few randomised studies, and the pooled review mixed heterogeneous pts, lesion sizes and techniques, both external beam and brachytherapy. Pooled LC from selected series is open to referral and reporting bias, and lesions treated with very few fractions in frail elderly pts may differ systematically from those given longer courses. Late cosmesis is the outcome that actually drives fractionation choice in pts under 70, and it is the endpoint these series capture least well. The piece offers nothing on it beyond a single case showing in-field hypopigmentation and epidermal atrophy at six months.

The more consequential claim sits in the Table 1 footnote: observation, not adjuvant RT, should be considered for most BCCs and low-risk SCCs. The author describes adjuvant indications as genuinely debated, so this is de-escalation by omission rather than by fractionation, and it carries a different failure mode. The exceptions are explicit and sensible: PNI fields that encompass neural structures, and high-risk lower lip SCC treated for curative intent and oral competence, where 20 or 25 fractions may be justified.

For the reader, the piece changes the default framing, not the evidence. It works as a departmental template linking schedule to age and ECOG. It does not settle whether hypofractionation preserves cosmesis in younger pts, or whether omitting adjuvant RT after excision is safe for anything beyond low-risk SCC. What would prove it wrong is a late-effect or recurrence signal appearing in exactly the younger and adjuvant populations the table extends hypofractionation into.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The bigger de-escalation is the Table 1 footnote favoring observation over adjuvant RT in most BCCs and low-risk SCCs. The schedule menu goes beyond RCR's trim (50 Gy in 15 fx instead of 55 Gy in 20 fx), with PNI fields and high-risk lower lip SCC kept at 20 or 25 fractions.

open_questions: Adjuvant RT vs observation after excision of BCC or low-risk SCC
Late cosmesis with hypofractionation in pts under 70

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion

A ≤1 mm GTV-PTV margin is only defensible with vendor 3D correction, higher readout bandwidth, ≤1 mm3 3D T1 and a short imaging interval.
studies.monday_clinic: In a brain-met pt whose planning MRI is ≥14 days old at SRS, the cited 6-month LC of 56% vs 95% questions planning off that scan; it does not define a threshold for fractionated courses, where repeat mid-course imaging is the separate question.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative review from Erlangen radiation oncology, radiology and neuroradiology, published alongside the DEGRO/DGMP stereotactic quality papers. No new patient data.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Frames MRI requirements against **GTV-PTV margins of ≤1 mm** in intracranial SRS. Recommends **vendor 3D distortion correction**, patient-specific active shimming and RT-optimized readout bandwidth, verified by phantom QA.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Consistent with the **2016 MRI-simulation consensus** (Paulson et al., Radiotherapy and Oncology): 3D vendor correction as minimum, higher bandwidth accepted at an SNR cost, <1 mm total distortion. Notes MPRAGE is the sequence in the standardized brain tumor imaging protocol (BTIP), while argues for T1-SPACE in RT planning.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case rests mostly on geometry: distortion, slice thickness and contrast timing all change the contour a planner draws. Only the imaging-interval data link an MRI parameter to **local control**; whether 3D correction or a SPACE sequence improves outcomes is untested.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Cited series are small (Seibert 28 lesions; Danieli 16 mets and 38 gliomas; Hessen 18 mets and 20 cavities). The **5-day interval** and repeat-imaging habits are Erlangen institutional practice, not tested thresholds.

studies.interpretation:
The argument here is less about MRI physics than about who owns the planning scan. A GTV-to-PTV margin of 1 mm or less assumes the image is geometrically faithful within that margin, yet the scan is often acquired by a diagnostic department optimizing for signal-to-noise and speed, with lower readout bandwidth and, in the authors' experience, only 2D vendor correction. The review's value is in translating those radiology defaults into geometric error a radiation oncologist can reason about: residual through-plane distortion up to 2 mm after 2D correction in their own example, and a simulated geographic miss in 8 of 28 lesions when Seibert and colleagues compared uncorrected with 3D-corrected images. Neither figure is an outcome, but against a 1 mm margin both exceed the error budget.

The one parameter tied to a clinical endpoint is the interval between imaging and treatment. Seymour's local control of 56% vs 95% at 6 months for intervals of 14 days or more is the most striking number in the paper, and the one a skeptic should handle most carefully. The source does not describe that study's design, and a long interval plausibly travels with other features (lesion size, growth rate, steroid changes, logistics in sicker pts) that would independently move control. Salkeld's management-change rates point the same way through the mechanism the authors emphasize, volume growth on re-imaging, which makes the biology plausible without isolating the interval as cause. The Erlangen 5-day ceiling is an institutional choice, not a tested threshold.

The sequence recommendation deserves similar calibration. Danieli's comparison favored T1-SPACE on contrast, conspicuity and GTV size, with MPRAGE missing 15.8% of metastases, and randomizing sequence order addresses the obvious contrast-timing confound. But the cohort was 16 metastases and 38 gliomas, and a larger GTV on one sequence does not prove the larger contour is the correct one. What the data support is that MPRAGE can understate enhancing extent, which matters most when a tight margin leaves no slack. The contrast-timing series from Yuh and Kushnisky make the same point from another angle: delay after gadolinium changes both detection and apparent volume, so contour size partly reflects acquisition protocol rather than tumor.

Against the 2016 MRI-simulation consensus the review is confirmatory rather than new: vendor 3D correction as a minimum, higher bandwidth accepted at an SNR cost, sub-millimeter total distortion, and phantom QA for residual error. Its practical contribution is naming where correction status lives in the DICOM header and explaining why 3 T is not automatically worse, given better shimming and SNR headroom for higher bandwidth.

What it leaves open is whether any of this moves outcomes. No cited study shows that 3D correction, higher bandwidth or a SPACE sequence changes local control or toxicity; the case rests on geometry. The authors concede it is unclear whether mask-immobilized MR simulation improves registration once current imaging standards are met, and the mid-course re-imaging data come from 18 metastases and 20 cavities over 3-5 fractions, too few to define a re-imaging trigger. For a department, the actionable read is an audit of its own external MRI protocols, not a change in prescription.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: External planning MRIs are often only 2D-corrected, leaving distortions up to 2 mm, and uncorrected images produced geographic miss in 8 of 28 lesions. A ≤1 mm GTV-PTV margin needs vendor 3D correction, higher bandwidth, ≤1 mm3 3D T1 and a short imaging interval to hold.

open_questions: Do distortion-correction and interval QA steps improve SRS local control?
Does mask-immobilized MR simulation improve registration under current imaging standards?
Does T1-SPACE contouring change outcomes, not just conspicuity?

📊 BCT for 2 or 3 foci: 6/204 LR, 3.1% at 5 yrs vs acceptability threshold <8%

Z11 likewise excluded third-field RT without reporting tangent axillary coverage: once dissection is dropped, field design carries the axilla.
studies.monday_clinic: In cT1-2 pts with 1-2 positive SLN undergoing lumpectomy with planned WBRT, Z11 10-yr data support omitting completion ALND; it does not extend to mastectomy pts, whom Z11 excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: NCCN 2023 Breast Cancer Congress talk, the surgical half of a locoregional session with SABCS 2022 updates. Covers **axillary management after 1-2 positive SLN**, **nodal staging after NAC**, breast-surgery omission after VACB, and **BCT for multiple ipsilateral breast cancer**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Z11 planned **whole breast RT** with third-field nodal RT excluded. AMAROS randomized **axillary RT vs AND**. The SABCS nodal-pCR cohort received **nodal RT in 78% (SLNB) vs 85% (TAD)**, and the multicentric BCT trial gave WBI with **RNI at physician discretion**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Z11 and AMAROS anchor current axillary practice after limited SLN positivity. The post-NAC data extend that logic to cN+ disease converted to nodal pCR, where the slides show **staging accuracy, not recurrence outcomes**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents cT1-2 pts having lumpectomy with 1-2 positive SLN, and cN+ pts reaching nodal pCR after NAC. Does not represent mastectomy pts under Z11, or BRCA carriers and neoadjuvant-treated pts considered for BCT with multiple foci.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The de-escalation case is strongest for Z11 at median 9.3 yrs; post-NAC staging rests on **FNR, a surrogate**, and the multicentric BCT data are single-arm. In each case, regional RT carries more of the axillary control as surgery recedes.

studies.interpretation:
The surgical half of this talk makes a consistent de-escalation argument, and its strongest part has the longest follow-up. ACOSOG Z11 at a median 9.3 years shows OS, DFS and locoregional recurrence that sit numerically on the SLNB side, even though 27% of the dissected arm had additional positive nodes. A radiation oncologist should not read that as residual axillary disease being harmless. Something other than surgery was controlling it. The slide states that third-field nodal irradiation was excluded, but it does not show how much of the low axilla the whole-breast tangents covered, and the trial cannot separate that variable from the surgical question. Applying Z11 to a pt planned for high tangents, standard tangents or partial breast irradiation means extrapolating from one dataset in different directions.

AMAROS supplies the randomized comparison of axillary RT against dissection that Z11 lacks, and it widens applicability to mastectomy, which Z11 excluded. Axillary recurrence is low in both arms (AND 0.43% vs ART 1.19% at 5 years), so the absolute difference is small. The practical message is about choosing between two forms of nodal treatment, not about whether nodal treatment matters. The slide gives 5-yr DFS of 86.9% vs 82.7% without a test statistic, so a reader should treat that gap as neither confirmed nor excluded.

The post-neoadjuvant section rests on diagnostic accuracy, not outcomes. In SENTINA, FNR falls from 24.3% with 1 SLN to 7.3% with 3 SLN, dual tracer reaches 8.6%, and TAD reaches 2.0%. All of these argue for a staging technique, but a false-negative rate measured against completion dissection is a surrogate: it counts disease left behind, not disease that recurs. The SABCS update moves toward outcomes in 1144 nodal-pCR pts, yet nodal RT was delivered to 78% and 85% of its two cohorts. Any axillary control that cohort shows comes from omitting dissection with regional RT in place. It cannot be read as support for omitting both.

The multicentric BCT data are the newest and least mature part of the talk. A 5-year LR of 3.1% clears the trial's <8% threshold. However, the subgroups that matter most for selection (pN1-3, close margins, pT2-3) have confidence intervals whose upper bounds exceed that threshold, and only 15 pts lacked MRI. RNI was at physician discretion, so the regional treatment the node-positive subgroup received was not standardized.

Across the talk, the decision moves the same way for a radiation oncologist. As surgery withdraws from the axilla, the RT plan becomes the regional treatment, and field design deserves the attention that the extent of dissection used to get.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: ALND omission after nodal pCR came with nodal RT in 78% (SLNB) and 85% (TAD), so axillary control there depends on regional RT. Z11 excluded third-field RT without reporting tangent axillary coverage, which leaves field design carrying the axilla once dissection is dropped.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Post-NAC staging accuracy depends on technique: SENTINA FNR 24.3% with 1 SLN vs 7.3% with 3 SLN, and TAD 2.0% vs SLNB alone 10.1%. Clipped-node retrieval and node count are the levers. BCT for 2 or 3 foci reached 3.1% 5-yr LR, but close margins carried 7.5%.

presentation.speaker: Jessica S. Young, MD
presentation.summary: The speaker argued that locoregional surgery is de-escalating on three fronts: the axilla, nodal staging after NAC, and multiple ipsilateral breast cancer. For 1-2 positive SLN with lumpectomy and WBRT, ACOSOG Z11 at 10 yrs shows no OS, DFS or locoregional penalty from omitting ALND, and AMAROS offers axillary RT as an alternative to dissection. After NAC, staging accuracy depends on technique: dual tracer, 3 SLN and clipped-node retrieval via TAD. BCT for 2 or 3 foci is presented as acceptable on a 5-yr LR of 3.1%.
critique: Z11 excluded third-field nodal RT, but the slides never show what axillary dose the whole-breast tangents delivered, so omitting ALND cannot be separated from the RT those pts received.
Post-NAC staging rests on false-negative rates against completion ALND, a surrogate for residual disease; the slides carry no axillary recurrence result for the 1144-pt nodal-pCR cohort.
The multicentric series is single-arm with 204 evaluable pts; close-margin and pN1-3 subgroups had 5-yr LR of 7.5% and 7.8%, with upper CI bounds of 26.5 and 22.2.
Z11 required lumpectomy and excluded mastectomy, so its result does not transfer to mastectomy pts; AMAROS covers them but compares axillary RT with dissection, not observation.

papers.title: Practical Considerations for Single Isocenter LINAC Radiosurgery of Multiple Brain Metastases
Magnetic resonance imaging for brain stereotactic radiotherapy
papers.abstract: Abstract Due to its superior soft tissue contrast, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for many radiotherapy treatment indications. This is especially true for treatment planning in intracranial tumors, where MRI has a long-standing history for target delineation in clinical practice. Despite its routine use, care has to be taken when selecting and acquiring MRI studies for the purpose of radiotherapy treatment planning. Requirements on MRI are particularly demanding for intracranial stereotactic radiotherapy, where accurate imaging has a critical role in treatment success. However, MR images acquired for routine radiological assessment are frequently unsuitable for high-precision stereotactic radiotherapy as the requirements for imaging are significantly different for radiotherapy planning and diagnostic radiology. To assure that optimal imaging is used for treatment planning, the radiation oncologist needs proper knowledge of the most important requirements concerning the use of MRI in brain stereotactic radiotherapy. In the present review, we summarize and discuss the most relevant issues when using MR images for target volume delineation in intracranial stereotactic radiotherapy.

papers.title: Implementing high-dose rate surface mould brachytherapy for carcinoma of eyelid: a practical approach and weekly review
papers.abstract: Surface mould brachytherapy is a conformal radiotherapy technique that can deliver high dose to the target while sparing nearby normal structures, Here, we aim to describe the procedurals details for high-dose rate (HDR) surface mould brachytherapy in sebaceous carcinoma of eyelid in a 54-year old lady. She was hesitant for surgery and any form of invasive intervention like interstitial brachytherapy. So, she was treated with surface mould HDR brachytherapy to a total dose of 52 Gy in 13 fractions at a dose of 4 Gy per fraction delivered twice daily using Iridium-192 isotope with no acute side effects. She was evaluated on a weekly basis for any radiation side effects and now she is disease-free for 6 months post-treatment with only mild dry eye. A detailed step-by-step procedure of surface mould technique, simulation procedure, dose prescription, planning, plan evaluation and treatment has been described in this paper. Surface mould HDR brachytherapy can be safely used as organ preserving modality of treatment for eyelid carcinoma.
